review:
The Way We All Go (2015), developed and published by ebi-hime, is a brief yet emotionally intense visual novel that prioritizes raw human vulnerability over traditional storytelling satisfaction. Rather than guiding players through a neatly structured narrative with clear resolutions, it presents a series of uncomfortable, intimate moments that revolve around flawed characters and the fragile connections between them. It’s not designed to entertain in a conventional sense—instead, it invites the player to sit with difficult emotions and observe how they unfold without interference.

The story centers on a small group of individuals whose lives intersect through strained relationships and unresolved personal issues. Instead of building toward a dramatic climax, the narrative is composed of quiet, often unsettling interactions that reveal deeper layers of insecurity, dependence, and emotional instability. The writing feels grounded in realism, capturing the awkwardness and tension of conversations where people struggle to express themselves or unintentionally hurt one another. There is a deliberate lack of exaggeration, which makes the characters feel believable, even when their behavior becomes frustrating or distressing.

One of the game’s most striking qualities is its refusal to impose judgment or provide clear moral direction. The characters are not framed as heroes or villains, and their actions are not neatly categorized as right or wrong. This ambiguity allows the story to feel more authentic, but it also makes it more challenging to engage with on an emotional level. Players are left to interpret the characters’ motivations and consequences on their own, which can lead to a more personal but also more uncomfortable experience.

Interactivity is minimal, even compared to most visual novels. Choices are rare and have little impact on the overall direction of the story, reinforcing a sense of inevitability. This lack of agency can feel limiting, but it also aligns with the themes of the game. The characters themselves often seem trapped by their circumstances and emotions, and the player’s inability to change events mirrors that lack of control. It shifts the experience from one of participation to one of observation, where the focus is on understanding rather than influencing.

Visually, the game adopts a simple anime-inspired style that emphasizes character expressions and subtle emotional cues. The artwork is not elaborate, but it is effective in conveying the tone of each scene. Small changes in posture or facial expression carry significant weight, helping to communicate feelings that are not always explicitly stated in the dialogue. The soundtrack complements this approach with subdued, melancholic tracks that reinforce the game’s somber atmosphere without overwhelming it.

The pacing is tightly controlled, with the entire experience unfolding over a relatively short period. There is little in the way of filler content, and each scene contributes to the overall emotional impact. However, the brevity also means that certain elements are left underdeveloped. While the characters are compelling, the limited runtime restricts how deeply their backgrounds and relationships can be explored. This can leave the story feeling incomplete, though it also adds to the sense of ambiguity that defines the game.

What ultimately sets The Way We All Go apart is its willingness to embrace discomfort. It does not offer easy resolutions or moments of relief, and it does not attempt to soften the consequences of its characters’ actions. Instead, it presents a snapshot of emotional struggle and leaves the player to process it independently. This approach can be difficult to engage with, especially for those expecting a more traditional narrative structure, but it also gives the game a distinct identity.

In the end, The Way We All Go (2015) is a deeply personal and introspective experience that prioritizes emotional honesty over conventional storytelling. It is not a game that aims to satisfy or entertain in the usual sense, but one that lingers through its tone and themes. For players willing to engage with its heavy subject matter and understated presentation, it offers a thought-provoking journey that stands out for its sincerity and restraint.

"This is a tale of misplaced love, a tale of a man searching for that misplaced love in all the wrong places, and how he gets his heart ripped out of his chest and stuck in his face so he can watch it slowly stop beating.”  The Insane Clown Posse – Toxic Love 

So what do those lyrics have to do with the game (The way we all go).. Well maybe nothing, or maybe everything.  It’s really hard to tell, I just think those lyrics go pretty hard, plus it’s the Insane Clown posse, as a 40+ year old man who lives on the fringes of society as an outcast, unloved, unwanted and treated like a POS, they were my go to band for many years, while I’ve only been to a single concert, I know that I’m truly a Juffalo.. errr a Juggalo..  

Maybe some better lyrics would have come from Huey Lewis and the News and the power of love “The power of love is a curious thing, make one man weep and another man sing”.  Anyway The Way we all go is sort of a visual novel about love..

The Story – You are Atcchan, a young man who was forced to leave his small town two years ago.  Much like the Beverly Hillbillies he was moving on up to the east side and he finally got a piece of that pie… I think.  Anyway Atcchan is coming back to his home town for a fun filled 3 day adventure, where he he’s planning on cracking some necks and cashing some checks.  He’s gonna be hunting that elusive beaver he missed out on years ago..  Wait a second this isn’t an adult visual novel, scrap that beaver comment.  Anyway back to the task at hand Atcchan has some choices to make, some hearts to possibly mend and some wrongs to make right.  Can he make all the right choices and heal the harm he’s caused, or will we be able to put him on the mess around and find out chart. 

Gameplay – it’s the normal visual novel gameplay, you press a button to move the story along, you can make choices throughout the story which will influence the eventual ending.  (game has 21 endings to be precise) 

Pro’s 
Decent enough story 
Easy (albeit time consuming) 100%
Fairly well written 
Lots of replay ability (although very repetitive) 
10 – 13 hours of content, (lots more if you don’t skip already seen text) 

Con’s 
Ultra repetitive
A tad bit long winded at times
Store page says Gore, but the gore is just a splash screen with red
A visual novel with no fap material ugh.

Recommendation - 
The content to price ratio is really good for 5.99 you’re getting easily 8 – 10 hours of content not including the skipping of already seen content which will tack on another couple of hours.  You can very easily get 100% for the game, and let’s be honest, most people just want that 100% baybay.  The game deals with some pretty heavy issues so if you’re triggered easily maybe you might want to avoid it, BUT, for the most part it’s just fluffy romantic visual novel content. Anyway, buy the game if you want an easy 100%, or just want to spend some time reading a decently written romantic visual novel..

I really wanted to like this game. I played about five of the routes and couldn't play any more.

The protagonist is so spineless that it's infuriating. The story is predictable, and at 200k words, a lot of the text just seems to be there to up the word count or make the game longer. It feels like it goes on forever, even if you've only played for a couple hours. Sometimes the forward skip doesn't even work.

If you want something similar but better, watch or play Higurashi. The premise is essentially the same: a male protagonist leaves his small village to move to the city and comes back a couple years later. They both have a lot of slice of life and light hearted scenes, while over all being a really dark game. Both have a yandere love interest and a tomboy love interest. While Higurashi is a lot longer, the first chapter is free on Steam currently and I found it a lot more interesting.

Overall, if you're looking for a cheap horror-esque visual novel to add to your library, there's better options. For the less than $2 I paid for it, I didn't have super high expectations, but I was still bored and disappointed.

I thought this VN deserved a more detailed review, so if you're interested in others like it, check out my Curator page here:

[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/35651135/] Val's Visual Novels, Anime & Hentai [/url]

[u][h1]Style[/h1][/u]
[u]Art[/u]
This was a VN made on a budget, sprites and characters are basic in terms of design, backgrounds and stuff used a lot of publicly available resources. But it's done decently, effort was made into making them fit together coherently as a whole, so I've no complaints. 

[u]Eroge Content[/u]
This has no eroge content.

[u][h1]Music and sound[/h1][/u]
As with art mentioned above, uses a lot of publicly available resources. I actually recognised one of the tunes from another VN I recently played, just because it's literally generic teen rock pop used for college/school setting VNs so often. 

[u][h1]Story[/h1][/u]
[u]Basics[/u]
I'm a writer. I look back at stuff I wrote long ago, and I always try my best to not be too hard on myself. We all start somewhere, and it's only with practice we get better. 

When I played this, I have to give full credit to the writer, they obviously put a lot more effort into this than I did with a lot of my first few works. I can tell. 

That said, effort alone doesn't make it great. But that's fine. 

The MC himself is awkward to the point that it's painful. Again, that's probably a good thing, since it was exactly how the author wanted the MC to be conveyed. The other characters had deep and detailed backstories, but they weren't quite lovable enough to get me invested. The humour was pretty basic, so it didn't get much of a laugh out of me. All these I can forgive. Writing's a craft you polish and improve.

But one thing I will point out I definitely didn't like is the large lack of agency I had over the ending of the stories. It fell into that trap of 'do things exactly like this, without knowing anything in advance, or else bad end or ending you didn't expect or like'. I really don't like that. 

[u][h1]Gameplay[/h1][/u]
Very standard VN fare, you get a few key choices, which each lead to an ending. Quite a few endings to be had if you go back and explore a bit more, but I found it hard to just because of how arbitrary some of the first few endings I got were. 

[u][h1]Summary[/h1][/u]
I wanted to give a neutral review, like you can on Curator pages. I wouldn't recommend it based on what it is, but I wanted to reflect in this review I appreciated it as a writer the effort that was put into making it, it wasn't some halfhearted effort thrown together just because. Full credit for that. Hopefully future works reflect on improvements made through experience.

[i]This was an experience I'd happily endure all over again and never tire of it like you do with watching your favourite TV programs or movies. My playtime just hit over 30hours but don't be deterred by that because it was spread out over 1-2 hours daily as I searched for all the many endings to this deeply entwined story.[/i]

The one thing that kept me returning to Ebi-Hime's VN was discovering each of the 21 endings complete with varying backstories and endings that, like all good Choices Matter genres, reflect off what route you take and with what characters.
I literally felt like I had discovered the VN equivalent of Russian Dolls where everytime you open one there is another hidden inside and, in this case, it is hidden discoveries of each character along with their unique traits that give added appeal to the depth of this VN.

The male protagonist is Atcchan, a meek & sensitive teen returning back to his hometown after a hiatus of 2years to stay with his grandparents and visit childhood friends. As with most VNs, the females each have their own personalities and there are 2 contrasting lead females called Amu and Noelle but the extra endings feature 4 more females that have their own side plots weaving into the main story linking the characters like a spiders web.
The writing is incredibly diverse ranging from emotional to dark themed to light humour depending on the characters involved; I enjoyed the descriptive nature of the writing that allowed the reader to get sucked into the plots and, at times, I wondered how much was creative writing and how much was taken or inspired from experience? The topics of regret, of emigrating leaving loved ones behind, cowardice (or is it selfishness?) and so many more emotions all explored in such a deep, honest way it truly does make you wonder where they originate from. If they are all creatively written that is a great accomplishment for a first VN.

With the variety of 21 endings, you'll be pleased to hear there is an autoskip which stops at the new plot areas so nothing can be missed and there are ample save slots if you aim to unlock all endings in a short time. Each ending uncovers an Achievement and, in-game, there is an Extras section in the menu to view unlocked artwork and a music gallery plus a list of the Ending titles for reference against Guides for players who use them to uncover the Achievements.
The artwork is rendered photo backgrounds with the anime character imposed and the characters do have a mix of facial expressions complete with sound effects for those funny moments. Again, for a first VN, this works well alongside the in depth writing style but for those who follow/play Ebi-Hime this area vastly improves in future releases both artistically and with the OST. (I previously played [u]Six Days of Snow[/u] and the two VNs are so drastically different which proves the diversity of Ebi-Hime's writing, ideas and personal drive to excel)

This game I think truly encompasses the saying "Quantity over quality." While I bought this visual novel due to the blood drop (signifiying that it was probably a lot darker than its steam page seemed) I feel like its potential was split into too many endings, leading to just a weaker overall game.

You play through most of the game as Attchan, a boy who has returned to his home village after moving with his family to the city. He's adjusted to city life, but there were friends from his village he left behind that he wants to see again. This leads to problems however...while he wrote to one best friend, Amu, after moving, he never said anything to his other best friend, Noelle. This regret grips him as he returns, and it becomes a driving point in several of the endings you can get.

While the writing does give the characters different voices, it is overall weak and poorly written most of the time, and the characterization is weakest in our protagonist. His feelings of regret and inner monologues are tedious to read through, and he has no personality beyond being the typical "nice guy" anime protagonist that you might see in a harem anime. His regret at never telling Noelle he was leaving is also never expanded upon in the first 10 endings, though there may be an ending where it goes into detail about it. Speaking of...

My biggest problem with this visual novel are the endings. 21 endings is indeed very ambitious, but it seems clear that ebi-hime spread the story too thin between all the endings, weakening the routes themselves. This further serves to just bloat the game with unnecessary details and even playthroughs - I love completing VN endings but trying to get all the endings of this game is [i]painfully boring[/i]. If you get all the endings, then I don't doubt it reveals a clearer picture of the story, or at least the characters, but some endings are quite confusing themselves as they pull in things that never really come up in the route (for example, [spoiler]one of the girls gets a yandere route, but it's never indicated she is unstable - instead, it's constantly commented she is just quiet. Her being yandere is important for several of the endings in the game.[/spoiler]).

I feel like it would have been better to consolidate some endings into the same route - that way, you get characters that are better written within the routes themselves and understand motivations that would lead to the specific ending, overall strengthening the writing. Furthermore, this avoids the many dark endings that clearly were written in order to shock the player, but fail as there is no sense of dread in the writing.

Aside from Attchan, Noelle and Amu (the maine heroines) are written OK when you consider the multiple endings, but they aren't stellar or memorable. I think that Noelle, despite being the main girl in promo material for the game, was a weaker character than Amu as her reasons for her actions are never quite as clearly explained as Amu, making her more confusing than understandable. Other characters that appear include Saki, Attchan's city friend, as well as two sisters that he went to high school with. They also have their own endings associated with them, even though they are mostly minor characters, which leads me back to my previous criticism of the multitude of endings as these endings are poorly written.

The presentation of the visual novel is rather bland, with stock background photos, music, sfx, and UI. It's the very basics of Ren'Py, and visually uninteresting. The art isn't great, and suffers from also being bland; this would be mitigated with good writing, but this VN unfortunately lacks that aspect as well.

Overall, a rather disappointing game given I was looking forward to its dark nature. There are other VNs of better quality in this price range on Steam (or free), so I don't recommend purchasing this.

It is a short visual novel heavily inspired by the Higurashi series in both aesthetic and writing. 
If you're a fan of Higurashi, you'll feel right at home. Even if you're not, it's a very enjoyable story with likable characters.

You should know that it's not a horror game, and the main feeling of this novel is actually... sadness.
There are two main characters to interact with and the whole game lasts for ~2 days, so the pacing is pretty tight.

The art is mediocre as this is a very budget work, especially the CGs, but the main characters' sprites do a fine work of conveying their emotions and after all I ended up really liking them. The backgrounds are slightly edited photographs - once again, it's almost an exact look of the Higurashi series, so this might be artist's choice.

The main characters are believable and deep enough, even more so in story segments when you can see the world from their eyes. The writing is subtle and very natural, Ebi-hime does a great work of not looking amateurish unlike most EVN writers out there. I particularly like how the writer operates the RenPy engine, uses NVL mode and paces the sentences so they always feel natural and comfortable to read. There's plenty of humour too, even though that's where I feel it borrows from Higurashi a little too much.

I admit the story didn't leave me too impressed like some other VNs out there, but I still felt that the game did a great work to convey its themes without going into tropes and cliches, and along with the quality prose it was overall a very enjoyable experience.

There are also an impressive amount of endings that make a short few hours novel into a pretty large work if you include all the possible branches. There aren't too many choices, but apparently most of them can branch the narrative and lead to different endings, which is somewhat uncommon for most VNs. I believe you won't feel like you completed the game and got to know the characters until you reach at least several endings. 
There is probably the best happy ending hidden somewhere, but I'm still miles away from reaching it!

+ It took me ~17 hours to 100% this game.  For $5.99, that is a great deal.

+ Each of the endings felt distinct.  None of them were low-effort as I'd expect when there's so many.  
+ The writing was free of grammatical errors.

- The writing often got very wordy.  There were many parts that I found myself speedreading through if only to get to the next piece of the plot.

When you run into someone after several years, your relationship doesn’t start from a clean slate again. It’s as if you were never gone in the first place, and it’s easy to fall into old routines - even if both parties have changed. 

How well do you really know those around you?

This is the main question that The Way We ALL GO (TWWAG) presents to the reader. Some may immediately be able to draw comparisons between TWWAG and Higurashi no Naku Koro ni. Both draw from this theme, both are in a small town, both involve the protagonist moving from the city, and both have some surprising dark twists. 

TWWAG and Higurashi are not carbon copies of one another. It is in the before mentioned question that they differ: while Higurashi’s main character must ask this question to friends made in the past several months, who he has seen face-to-face for almost half a year before the game begins, TWWAG’s protagonist must ask this question about those that, two years ago, he called friends. For three days, he can rekindle relationships with those he has not seen in two years. Can he still call himself a friend?

You have three days. Make the most of them.

Superb visual novel (adventure for people who don't know the genre), yanderes and all.

At fist I thought this was gonna be a bloody ride, as I got the cruelest endings, but there's room for a lot. Romance? Yup. Tenderness? Indeed. Creepy things? It's in the game.

I sincerely praise the writer, he managed to create natural dialogues that flow like a river... with some references to geekdom thrown in... and finally... adolescents who behave like adolescents: more often than not they won't have a clue, they do clumsy and downright stupid things, and love is too much to handle for them. Now this is very much so more realistic than your average visual novel.

Although set in Japan, this could be anywhere, since it has a more Western feel than most visual novels. At least the characters seem more... relatable. Their mindsets and ideas are also more in line with us Westerners.

I'd recommend it even to those who don't know what a visual novel is, or newcomers to the genre. Not exactly an RPG, if you don't know what you'll find, go with "branching adventure with 21 possible endings". The only means of gameplay is reading, selecting choices and clicking to make the text progress (I personally use the "Return" key). Not exactly Call of Duty material.

The Way We All Go (TWWAG for short) is a visual novel that may seem short for the first playthrough, but is actually quite long due to all different outcomes and endings you can achieve. Of course, my playtime is also affected by the fact I did not use a guide (meaning many attempts at getting different endings failed), but even if you do use one, you will certainly still be in for many hours of reading.

Although the story does contain its fair share of anime cliches (the Onodera sisters being the epitome of that, with one being a siscon and the other, a himedere), I would not really say yandere is one of them. That is because, although many of the 21 endings [i]are[/i] yandere-ish, most are well written. They are clearly not there just for the fanservice, for people to squee over a heartbroken girl turned obsessive badass. They make sense. And let's be honest, it is very hard to find well-written yanderes that make sense.

The reason why they make so much sense lies in Noelle's backstory, which is related to one of ebi-hime's biggest strengths in writing: her portrayal of mental illness. Noelle's problems and Atcchan's anxiety (and awkwardness), much like the main character's depression in Asphyxia, are conveyed extremely well, in a realistic manner that makes you think Noelle's actions under so much pressure are not that unexpected. 

Although the plot isn't stellar, the characters and variety of endings definitely make TWWAG shine. Of course it has its flaws--as I said, the Onoderas are a little too stereotypical for me (which makes them the opposite of Noelle and Atcchan in terms of depth, imo), there is a fair share of cliches, some parts in writing make it sound like a translation (...even though it's not), and I also find the art to be a large downside of the novel (sprites may be okay if you're into the overly anime look, but most CGs except for the chibi ones are subpar, with stiff lines, poor shading and no dynamism at all). But despite its flaws, it is a good novel and a very interesting experience for those who like thinking of how one small action (or choice!) may lead to an entirely different outcome. 7/10

Short, and is constantly being portrayed as a guy that overthinks things, does the nervous stutter, and is blushing more times than not. I personally never found nervous stutter cute, especially not when it is written into the text, and really wish he would cut it out, as it does nothing for his character or the story. Secondly there is his overthinking, which draws out some things way too long especially before the story starts to really get going...

If we are presented with a shocking piece of information, we don't need to read all the scenarios he could think of in order to realize he is worried and overthinking it. It would be nice if the reader was the one that got to think about possible reasons instead of him. :P Kinda the fun of reading is guessing ahead, or trying to pull out the deeper meaning of mundane things in a story, but it gets a bit annoying when the protagonist is doing it. I don't want to constantly read the protagonists weird guesses. [spoiler]Especially because he overthinks something as simple as his grandma trying to get him to eat big meals... I mean I sometimes feel bad about my grandma constantly putting food and candy on the table, but that is because it hard to say no without her just starting to look for something else for me to eat. I find it bizarre to start coming up with reasons as to why "Grandma might be punishing him" with big meals...[/spoiler] Sometimes in a story writting less gives a bigger impact. For example the six-word novel "For Sale: Baby shoes, never worn" I feel some of the impact would be pulled out if that was followed by the writer listing six different possibilities for such an ad. :P

I also think he is a jerk... [spoiler]Seriously, leaving your best friend without even telling her, and not contacting her at all for two years? Without any reason beyond it is uncomfortable to say... That is not "Oh he is just shy, and cute. He hates conflicts." No. That is "What an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥..." levels of douchebagery. I mean I didn't stay in contact with anyone I went to school with, but that is because they were acquaintances or weak friendships at best, and my best childhood friend was my cousin... So I might not be able to relate to moving away like that. But still... That is just so low... I wouldn't blame her if she had kicked him in the balls for that move. It would be well earned.[/spoiler]

But once the story gets going and we get introduced to some of the female characters, the story becomes more enjoyable and there comes a bigger emotional investment. I feel the supporting and secondary casts' personalities and behavior is really what pulls this experience up from being a negative one. They are far more interesting than the main lead. [spoiler]I did feel sad and angry hearing about the torments in one of the girls' back story. Which is good, as it shows that I was invested despite the novel's rocky start.[/spoiler]

So yeah, the story is slow, but that is what is to be expected when it relies more on text.

When one thinks of a visual novel what comes to mind? A lot of reading, cute girls, little to no actual gameplay, if it’s not Kinetic then choices that lead to 3-10 different endings. Throw that last one out the window. Yes there are endings, but there aren’t 3-10, there’s 21. You heard that right, there are 21 endings in total and it took me around 16-17 hours to get them all (with some help from a guide of course).

The Way We All Go or TWWAG, which is much easier to type, is a story about a 16 year old boy named Attchan who returns to his hometown after a few years of city living. He's back for a three-day visit to see his grandparents as well as two of his best friends, Noelle and Amu. When he moved he never said goodbye to one of his good friends, Noelle, and once he moved, he wrote letters to Amu but not to Noelle. Once he arrives he’s stuck with the choice of if he tries just having fun with Amu, facing his fears and apologizing to Noelle, or hanging out with an old classmate he never talked to before.

Since you’ve only got three days, and you need to make the most of it, you can’t address the various problem that have arose thanks to Atcchan’s cowardice and his disappearance for the past couple years. The obvious choice is to apologize to Noelle and see if you can make up for ditching her without a word, but in true VN style you don’t necessarily have to do that, choosing instead to spend time with Amu or others. There’s a wide variety of endings to go for; this is a horror VN to some extent, and given it’s a VN along with the basic plot description I just offered, you can probably guess what happens in several of them. Definitely not the way to go, Attchan.

TWWAG is also similar to Higurashi not just in themes and setting but also in artwork. More rather, in the original Higurashi artwork. Due to time, skill and money constraints, lower quality art assets were used in Higurashi. Many people are put-off by this style, preferring to read something with both reasonable story and reasonable artwork. Back now to TWWAG. For the CG, the art styles vary between each due to having multiple artists. Some of them are a decent quality but most are not. Likewise with a few of the character sprites – the grandparents are closer to the expected art quality. The game isn’t voice acted which isn’t a problem. It also uses stock music (as can be seen by an “artist” for 3 of the songs being “freestockmusic”) which is okay for the most part, with the exception of one track in particular. (You'll know which one it is when you hear it)

I have mixed feelings on this visual novel. Overall, I'll say that I do like it, but there are definitely some flaws. 

The art really bothered me. I think it clashes a lot. The background images look like pictures that were converted on an app to look like paintings. Putting anime-style character art over realistic images looks so out of place and visually unappealing. I did like the CG images though, especially the chibi stuff. 

At first I was really bored with the story. It was mundane; since I wasn't familiar with the characters, their trivial banter felt like a chore to read through. However, once I got to the first ending (out of 21 endings), I realized that it was probably intentionally mundane to make the ending(s) even more surprising/shocking. The reader might feel that it's just an average slice-of-life kind of story, but get rudely awoken once they reach the first ending. I certainly did get a shock when I found out that [spoiler]Noelle has some serious psychological issues that cause her to become a psychopath[/spoiler] if you don't make the right choices in the VN. The choices in the game definitely affect the outcome of the ending. Going through all 21 endings was very entertaining and interesting. The last one, #21, was my favorite, because it included all possible characters that can be encountered during the story. 

The characters become more likeable once they're developed. During my first playthrough, I found the two main female characters a bit dull. However, through several playthroughs, various different information is revealed about them, particularly Noelle, and they become more interesting. Noelle is by far my favorite character of the story, because I can relate to her life experiences a bit; however, I can't say that I like her entirely, because it's difficult to like someone who [spoiler]killed innocent, defenseless bunnies[/spoiler]. I couldn't stand the protagonist. Even after going through all the endings, I just couldn't get past how passive, boring, and dumb he is. 

Overall, I recommend this visual novel. Bear through the first playthrough and get to the first ending, at least, before deciding whether it's for you or not.
